prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and its development into atomic clocks at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B031, Katori and Ye) as my preferred configuration, unchanged from round 1. After reading all eight statements the case looks stronger to me on one point: the people who rank it first (Kroll, Lindroth) are the two members who can judge the physics directly, and the objections raised against it, lineage and the unredefined second, concern framing and timing and not whether the result is real. The discovery-or-invention test is met by a single identifiable idea, the magic-wavelength condition that lets many neutral atoms be trapped without shifting the clock transition, followed by an accuracy programme that reached about 1e-18 and has been reproduced by independent laboratories. The two-name credit is compact and no member has proposed a different pair. I would word the citation around the lattice scheme and its demonstrated accuracy, so that it says what is new compared with the comb and with single-ion control.
statement.case_against: The most serious point is the one Kroll, Danielsson, Pearce and Lindroth all raised: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover the neighbouring advances, and a third award for the same measurement ecosystem could look like a continuation. Second, Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Gill and the ion-clock groups lie outside a two-name credit, and the first lattice-clock demonstrations have a priority history I cannot settle from the shortlist. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so Danielsson's reading that the decisive payoff is still prospective has some force. Against that, circuit QED has the broadest support and a three-name split that is at least as clean, so if the committee concludes that the lineage argument is decisive, B016 is the better lead and I would accept it.

responses.point: Circuit QED is a defined discovery with a defined date, mature after two decades, with a clean allocation of one theory name and two experimental groups, and my reading of 2025 as evidence of openness to the field counters the sequencing worry.
responses.response: You quoted my reading of 2025 as openness, and I still hold it, but I did not mean it to settle the overlap question. The test the chair posed is whether strong coupling and dispersive readout is a discovery distinct from macroscopic quantum tunnelling, and I think it is a reasonable yes: one concerns the quantum behaviour of a circuit variable, the other concerns coherent exchange between a circuit and a single photon. My remaining difficulty is that Danielsson, Eriksson and Kroll read it as an enabling architecture, and you disclosed that you direct a centre built on it. I therefore give weight to your technical account of dispersive readout and the bus, but not to your estimate of how others will see the overlap. I keep B016 as my first alternative and I would not resist it if the committee preferred it.

responses.point: Circuit QED should lead because it is a single sharply defined idea, its originality is not in doubt, and the trio fits the three-laureate limit; he would keep the citation narrow to strong coupling and dispersive readout so that Girvin, Huang and Devoret are not forced in.
responses.response: A narrow citation is the right answer to the chair's question about Girvin and Huang, and I would use the same method for B031, naming the lattice scheme and its accuracy and leaving the many ion and lattice groups out of the wording. But a narrow citation does not remove the omission, it only hides it, and Girvin co-authored the founding proposal. I read that as a larger attribution cost than the two-name clock credit, where one person proposed the scheme and the other drove the accuracy frontier. You say seven of eight rank B016 in the top four, which I accept as a weak signal of safety, but it is also true that B031 is the only candidate all eight of us ranked. On discovery versus invention I do not agree that it separates B016 from B031, since both are inventions with measurable consequences.

responses.point: The magic-wavelength proposal removes the conflict between tight trapping and a clean clock transition, with 10^-18 accuracy, geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second as concrete consequences, while the lineage from Hall's 2005 prize and ion clocks is the main reservation.
responses.response: I agree with your account of the Lamb-Dicke condition and the many-atom averaging, and I accept that the lineage is the main reservation. I would not lean on the redefinition of the second as a reason for timing, as you do, because the discovery stands on comparisons near 1e-18 between independent laboratories whatever the CIPM decides, and an argument tied to a pending decision could look weak if the decision slips. Your disclosure about Hall's laboratory is relevant to how the committee treats lineage, since you are well placed to say what is genuinely new beyond the comb. On Lemonde, Lisdat and the ion groups I would not add names, but I want the citation to name the scheme so that nobody reads it as a prize for optical clocks in general.

responses.point: The lattice clock combines a clear original idea with an experimental programme that reached about 10^-18, the credit is compact between Katori and Ye, and the atomic-structure physics of polarisabilities and systematic shifts is solid and demanding rather than incremental.
responses.response: This is the judgement I rely on, because atomic structure is outside my training. In round 1 I asked whether lattice clocks are the leading route to the redefinition or one route among several, and ion clocks reaching comparable accuracy make me careful about that, so I will not argue from the redefinition. What I do ask is that you say whether the magic-wavelength condition is the new physics here or whether single-ion clocks achieve the same end by another route. If the first holds, the answer to the lineage objection is that the lattice clock gives many-atom interrogation and the stability that follows, which a single ion does not. I also note your own caution about overweighting your first place, which I think is correct and which I apply to my own first choice B009.

responses.point: Pearce, now ranking circuit QED first, asks whether the Krivanek STEM-corrector question is a bar to aberration-corrected TEM or only a refinement of the citation.
responses.response: You asked directly, so I will answer. I think the STEM-corrector line is more than a refinement: Krivanek and Dellby achieved a working corrector in STEM in parallel, and any Rose, Haider, Urban trio will be read as passing them over. Together with Johansson's and Kroll's point about whether an electron microscopy prize sits in physics after the Ruska precedent, that is why I do not press B009 as a lead, and I am conflicted on it in any case. I also take your point that your first-place ranking of circuit QED and my second place are closer than the opening ballots show. Where we still differ is on how much weight the 2025 circuit prize deserves, which you treat as the main exposure to be managed and I treat as manageable but real.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts lattice clocks as a distinct discovery after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether a two-name credit for Katori and Ye is defensible given Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Gill and the ion-clock groups.
Whether the 2025 circuit prize makes B016 too close, which decides how B016 and B031 rank against each other.
Whether Girvin's role as co-author of the founding proposal breaks the B016 trio.
Whether the STEM-corrector line and the question of electron microscopy as physics rule out B009 in any cycle.
statement.conflict_note: My conflict disclosure is unchanged. I work in transmission electron microscopy and am president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so B009 is my own field and I would recuse myself from it, which is why it is only an alternative. I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and have long-running exchanges with Japanese universities, and Katori is at the University of Tokyo, so that institutional connection should be considered for B031, although I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. Goran Johansson is my Chalmers colleague, and he directs a centre related to B016, which is not my own conflict but bears on how his support for that candidate is weighed.
